messages.content: Analyze this sentence.  "Consydre thou myne condicyon; reflecte upon myne fader. Shall I forsake hym, when he is strycken wyth blyndnesse and destytute, to wrastle wyth infirmitie and penurye, when it lyeth wythin my poure to rendre hys latter yeeres fylled wyth comforte and joye?" Each paragraph of your response must end with the same word it started with, separate paragraphs with a newline.

message.content:
This sentence is an archaic English plea that asks the addressee to weigh the speaker’s circumstances and the father’s suffering. It presents abandonment as a moral failure because the father is blind, poor, and near the end of life. The rhetorical question heightens the speaker’s appeal to duty and conscience. This

Modern English would read it as: Consider my condition; reflect upon my father. Should I forsake him when he is struck with blindness and destitute, struggling with infirmity and poverty, when it lies within my power to fill his later years with comfort and joy? Modern

The spellings are old English in form: Consydre, myne, fader, forsake, hym, strycken, wyth, blyndnesse, destytute, wrastle, infirmitie, penurye, poure, rendre, latter, yeeres. These forms mark the line as literary or historical rather than ordinary modern English. They also give the plea a solemn, elevated tone. The

Grammatically it addresses the listener directly, then moves from a command to a question. The clause after the semicolon urges reflection on the father, and the question frames abandonment as an impossible choice. The final clause explains that the speaker can provide comfort in the father’s remaining years. Grammatically

Thematically it opposes neglect with care, and it uses physical suffering to make an ethical demand. The father’s blindness and poverty create urgency, while the phrase filled with comfort and joy suggests the speaker’s desired act of mercy. The sentence is therefore an argument for loyalty to a vulnerable parent. Thematically
